mainTopic: Is a blemished animal set aside for offerings like unallocated money (מעות סתומים)? רב המנונא and רבא challenge רב נחמן using ברייתות about a son using his father's offerings.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier answer: an animal fit for a חטאת cannot be offered as an עולה, because a חטאת is female and an עולה is male, so such animals already count as allocated. רב המנונא then challenges רב נחמן's rule that a blemished animal is like מעות סתומים. He quotes a ברייתא about a father and son who were both נזירים. In that ברייתא, the father's unallocated money goes to נדבה, while each set-aside animal is treated by its type. The גמרא first answers that the ברייתא means only an unblemished animal. It then asks why the ברייתא didn't simply say 'a blemished animal goes to נדבה.' The answer is that a blemished animal is holy only for its value, so it is already included in 'money.' רבא then opens a new objection from a ברייתא that learns from 'קרבנו' that a son cannot use his father's חטאת, even when their sins match. That ברייתא goes on to suggest that a father's money, unlike his animal, might be usable, just as in נזירות, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A sin-offering animal can't become a burnt-offering
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes an earlier answer. An animal fit for a חטאת cannot be offered as an עולה, because a חטאת is female and an עולה is male. So each animal is already tied to its own offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really say that this animal, which is for a חטאת, should be offered as an עולה? This one is female and that one is male!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up its answer to an earlier question. It points out that a female animal fit for a חטאת could never be brought as an עולה, which must be male.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the animals are naturally suited to different offerings, setting them aside is like labeling each one. That makes them unlike a blemished animal or a silver bar, which are not suited to any one offering and so count as מעות סתומים.

keyTerms.meaning: Can you really say...? (a way of rejecting an idea)
Sin-offering; for a נזיר it is a female sheep
Burnt-offering; for a נזיר it is a male sheep
Female / male

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the end of an earlier argument, not a new topic. It explains why animals of different kinds count as 'allocated' even if the owner never said which animal is for which offering.

phrases.english: Can you really say
that this one, which is for a sin-offering, will be offered as a burnt-offering?
Here it is female, here it is male.
phrases.notes: A נזיר's חטאת is a female lamb and his עולה is a male lamb, so they can't be swapped.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer to a question asked before this section begins.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: animals suited to different offerings count as allocated.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might have thought that unlabeled animals are like unallocated money.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since a חטאת must be female and an עולה male, each animal is already tied to its offering.

steps.title: רב המנונא questions the blemished-animal rule
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא raises an objection: do we really say that a blemished animal is like unallocated money?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא objected: Do we really say that a blemished animal is like unallocated money?
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא opens a challenge against רב נחמן's rule that a blemished animal counts like מעות סתומים. The proof for his challenge comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן treated a blemished animal like money, since it can't be offered itself and is only sold for its value. רב המנונא doubts this and is about to bring a source that seems to treat every animal as allocated.

keyTerms.meaning: A blemished animal, which cannot be brought as an offering
Is like unallocated (money)

phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna raised an objection:
And do we really say
that a blemished animal is like unallocated funds?
phrases.notes: This is the rule of רב נחמן from before this section.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the earlier answer to directly challenge רב נחמן's rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's rule that a blemished animal is like מעות סתומים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A source will show that animals, apparently including blemished ones, are treated as allocated.

steps.title: The ברייתא about a son and his father's נזירות
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא quotes a ברייתא about a father and son who were both נזירים. The father set aside money for his offerings and died, and the son vowed to be a נזיר on condition that he could use his father's money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: In what case did they say that a man shaves using his father's נזירות? When he and his father were both נזירים, and the father set aside money for his נזירות and died, and the son said, 'I am a נזיר on condition that I shave using Father's money.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא is setting up his proof by quoting the case from a ברייתא. The part that matters for his question comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Shaving' here means bringing the offerings that end a נזירות. The case is about what happens to things the father set aside for his offerings, which leads into how the ברייתא sorts money versus animals.

keyTerms.meaning: Shaves; here it means bringing the offerings at the end of נזירות
The state of being a נזיר
Set aside (for an offering)
On condition that

phrases.english: Come and hear:
How did they say
that a man shaves for his father's naziriteship?
phrases.notes: 'Shaves' means he brings his end-of-נזירות offerings using what his father set aside.

phrases.english: When he and his father were both nazirites,
and his father set aside money for his naziriteship
and died, and the son said: 'I am hereby a nazirite'

phrases.aramaic: עַל מְנָת שֶׁאֲגַלֵּחַ עַל מְעוֹת אַבָּא״.
phrases.english: on condition that I shave with Father's money.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for רב המנונא's objection.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a blemished animal counts as allocated
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a son who vows to use his father's נזירות money

steps.title: The ברייתא splits money from animals
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says unallocated money goes to נדבה, while each set-aside animal is treated by its type: the חטאת dies, the עולה is an עולה, the שלמים are שלמים. רב המנונא argues that this must include even blemished animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the father had unallocated money, it goes to נדבה. If he had a set-aside animal: a חטאת is left to die, an עולה is offered as an עולה, and שלמים are offered as שלמים. Doesn't this include even a blemished animal?
steps.whatsHappening: Here is the heart of רב המנונא's proof. The ברייתא only splits money from animals, so he argues that every animal, even a blemished one, counts as allocated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a blemished animal were like unallocated money, the ברייתא should have put it with the money that goes to נדבה. Since it speaks of animals in general, it seems to treat all animals as allocated, which goes against רב נחמן.

keyTerms.meaning: Unallocated money, not assigned to any one offering
They go to the communal fund for voluntary offerings
It must be left to die
Peace-offering
Isn't it...? (introduces a suggested reading)

phrases.english: If he had unallocated funds,
they go to gift offerings.
If he had a set-aside animal:
one for a sin-offering must die.
One for a burnt-offering is offered as a burnt-offering,
and peace-offerings are offered as peace-offerings.
Isn't this so even for a blemished animal?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא and draws the inference against רב נחמן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's rule that a blemished animal is like מעות סתומים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא contrasts only money with animals, so it seems all animals, even blemished ones, count as allocated.

steps.title: No: the ברייתא means an unblemished animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the ברייתא is talking only about an unblemished animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about an unblemished animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב נחמן by reading the ברייתא's 'animal' as an unblemished one only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An unblemished animal can be offered itself, so it counts as allocated. A blemished one might still be like money, so the ברייתא doesn't have to be read against רב נחמן.

keyTerms.meaning: Unblemished (animal), fit to be offered

phrases.english: No, it means an unblemished animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggested reading of the ברייתא from step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the claim that the ברייתא includes blemished animals.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as speaking only of unblemished animals.

steps.title: Then why didn't the ברייתא mention a blemished animal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges that answer. If a blemished animal is like unallocated money, the ברייתא should have said 'a blemished animal goes to נדבה' instead of contrasting animals with money.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is a blemished animal really like unallocated money? If so, why does the ברייתא bring up money specifically? Let it say: if he had a blemished animal, it goes to נדבה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 5. If a blemished animal belonged with the money, the ברייתא would have used it as its example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A clearer contrast would have been between two animals, unblemished versus blemished. That would have taught the rule for money by extension. Since the ברייתא chose money instead, it suggests that a blemished animal is not like money.

keyTerms.meaning: Why specifically this? Why pick this example?
Let it say

steps.confusionAlert: The question is about the ברייתא's choice of wording. The גמרא is not asking about the law of money; it asks why the ברייתא didn't pick the closer example of a blemished animal.

phrases.english: But is a blemished animal like unallocated funds?
Why mention money specifically?

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא: הָיְתָה לוֹ בְּהֵמָה בַּעֲלַת מוּם
phrases.english: Let it say: if he had a blemished animal,
it goes to gift offerings!
phrases.notes: The animal itself can't be offered, so this means its value goes to the נדבה fund.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 5 by looking at how the ברייתא is worded.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading in step 5 that the ברייתא speaks only of unblemished animals
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If blemished animals were like money, the ברייתא would have contrasted unblemished and blemished animals, not animals and money.
steps.whyThisMatters: This puts רב נחמן's rule under pressure again. The next step answers it by showing that a blemished animal is already included in 'money'.

steps.title: A blemished animal is really just money
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the point of step 6. The ברייתא's 'money' already includes a blemished animal, because a בעלת מום is only holy for its value, and value is money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, that is exactly so. What is a blemished animal holy for? For its value. And value is money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 6. It says a blemished animal does not need its own mention, because it already counts as 'money'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 asked why the ברייתא contrasted animals with money instead of saying 'a blemished animal goes to נדבה'. The answer is that a בעלת מום cannot be offered, so its holiness is really only in its value. That means it is already included in the word 'money'. So רב המנונא's proof fails, and a blemished animal can still be treated like unallocated money.

keyTerms.meaning: an animal with a blemish, which cannot be brought on the מזבח
is made holy, consecrated
its value, its worth in money
yes, that is so: accepting the point being made

steps.whatToRemember: A blemished animal is holy only for its money value, so in this ברייתא it counts as 'money' and goes to נדבה.

phrases.english: Yes, that is so,
what is a blemished animal made holy for?
For its value, and value is money.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי, בַּעֲלַת מוּם לְמַאי קַדִּישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by accepting its premise and showing that 'money' already includes a blemished animal.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefinition: a blemished animal is placed inside the category of money.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If a blemished animal were like money, the ברייתא should have named it separately.
steps.terutzMaskana: No separate mention is needed. A בעלת מום is holy only for its value, so it is already included in 'money'.

steps.title: רבא opens a new objection using the word 'his offering'
steps.stepSummary: רבא begins a new challenge to the idea that a blemished animal is like money. He quotes a ברייתא: from 'קרבנו', a person fulfills his duty only with his own offering, not his father's. The ברייתא first suggests that this might only apply when the sins are of different severity.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: 'His offering' teaches that a person fulfills his duty with his own offering, not with his father's. One might have thought he cannot use his father's offering only when it was set aside for a lighter sin and he needs it for a more severe one, or the reverse.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא is opening a new objection by starting to quote a ברייתא. This step is only the setup: we have not yet seen how it attacks the earlier view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from the word 'קרבנו' that a son cannot use his father's חטאת. It first offers a narrow reading: maybe this only applies when the two sins do not match, light for severe or severe for light. The ברייתא will narrow and refine this step by step.

keyTerms.meaning: 'his offering', the word in the פסוק that the ברייתא builds on
fulfills his obligation
a lighter sin / a more severe sin
one might have thought: introduces a possible mistake

phrases.english: רבא raised an objection:
"His offering": with his own offering he fulfills his duty,
and he does not fulfill it with his father's offering.

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל לֹא יֵצֵא בְּקׇרְבָּנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו
phrases.english: One might think he cannot fulfill his duty with his father's offering
only when it was set aside for a lighter sin and he needs it for a more severe one,
or set aside for a more severe sin and he needs it for a lighter one,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב המנונא's objection is answered, רבא starts a fresh objection on the same question from a different ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a blemished animal is like unallocated money.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Not yet stated. רבא is laying out the ברייתא, and the inference against the view comes later.

steps.title: Even when the sins match, the father's offering does not work
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rejects the narrow reading. Because 'קרבנו' is written twice, a son cannot use his father's offering even when both sins are equally light or equally severe.
steps.simpleTranslation: But one might think he can use an offering his father set aside for a light sin for his own light sin, or for a severe sin for his own severe sin. So the verse says 'his offering', 'his offering': he fulfills his duty with his own offering, and not with his father's.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and widens the rule. Even matching sins do not let the son use his father's offering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second 'קרבנו' teaches that the ban is complete. The father's offering does not work for the son even when the sins match exactly. The ברייתא is building a full rule about the father's set-aside animal before it turns to money.

keyTerms.meaning: the verse teaches: introduces the פסוק that settles the question
set aside an animal or money for an offering

phrases.english: but he can fulfill his duty with an offering his father set aside
for a light sin, when he needs it for a light sin,
or for a severe sin, when he needs it for a severe sin.
So the verse says: "his offering", "his offering".
phrases.notes: ויקרא 4:23 and 4:28. The word appears twice, and the second one widens the rule.

phrases.english: With his own offering he fulfills his duty,
and he does not fulfill it with his father's offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted by רבא, rejecting the narrow reading from step 8.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a son can never use his father's set-aside offering animal.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The double word 'קרבנו' in ויקרא 4:23 and 4:28.

steps.title: A father's animal does not work, but maybe his money does
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא now suggests a split. A father's set-aside animal cannot be used, just as a נזיר cannot use his father's animal. But maybe money the father set aside can be used even for a different sin, just as a נזיר may use his father's money.
steps.simpleTranslation: One might think he cannot use an animal his father set aside, even for matching sins, light for light or severe for severe, because a person cannot bring his נזיר offerings with his father's animal. But maybe he can use money his father set aside, even severe for light or light for severe, because a person can bring his נזיר offerings with his father's money.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues, contrasting a father's animal with a father's money. The amud ends here in the middle of the ברייתא; its ruling and רבא's point come on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא borrows a known rule from נזירות: a son can use his father's money but not his father's animal. It asks whether the same split applies to חטאת. This sharp line between animal and money is what רבא will use to question whether a blemished animal really counts as money.

keyTerms.meaning: shaves: here it means bringing the נזיר's offerings when he finishes his נזירות
for נזירות, the period of being a נזיר
an animal
money
since, because: gives the reason

steps.confusionAlert: This part of the ברייתא is still in 'יכול' mode, 'one might think'. The money half is a possibility being raised, not the final ruling.

phrases.english: One might think he cannot fulfill his duty with his father's offering
when it is an animal that his father set aside,
even light sin for light sin,
or severe sin for severe sin,
since a person cannot shave
with his father's animal for נזירות,
phrases.notes: 'Shave' here means bringing the נזיר's offerings. This matches the father-and-son נזיר ברייתא from steps 3 and 4.

phrases.english: but he can fulfill his duty with money his father set aside,
even severe sin for light sin,
or light sin for severe sin,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֲרֵי אָדָם מְגַלֵּחַ עַל מְעוֹת אָבִיו בִּנְזִירוּת,
phrases.english: since a person can shave with his father's money for נזירות,

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל לֹא יֵצֵא בְּקׇרְבַּן אָבִיו בִּבְהֵמָה שֶׁהִפְרִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, moving from the father's animal to the father's money by comparison with נזירות.
steps.raayaObject: A possible split between a father's set-aside animal, which cannot be used, and his set-aside money, which perhaps can.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The נזירות rule that a son may shave with his father's money but not with his father's animal.
